problem: Existing reconstruction-based 3D indoor datasets (Matterport3D, ScanNet, Gibson, Stanford 2D-3D-S) have geometry and texture artifacts, missing surfaces, 8-bit LDR colours and no mirror or glass modelling. Their semantics come from Felzenszwalb pre-segmentation, which gives inaccurate object boundaries. Synthetic CAD datasets (SUNCG, InteriorNet) lack real-world clutter and imperfections. All of this widens the sim-to-real gap for embodied agents trained in these scenes.
motivation: Simulators such as AI Habitat allow faster-than-realtime, parallel training of embodied agents for navigation, instruction following and EQA, but transfer to the real world depends on how realistic the simulated scenes are visually, geometrically and semantically. The authors argue that near-photorealistic replicas of real spaces are needed. Unlike static image datasets, 3D replicas support active perception, because views can be rendered from any pose.
key_idea: Release a small set of very high-fidelity real-world indoor reconstructions (dense meshes, HDR PTex textures, planar mirror and glass reflectors, primitive-level semantic class and instance labels) captured with a custom RGB-D rig and cleaned manually. The scenes are exported to be natively usable in AI Habitat.
insight: The paper trades scale for fidelity. Table 1 reports median geometry resolution of 6k primitives/m² vs 0.7k for Matterport3D, with comparable colour resolution (92k vs 97k pixels/m²). Replica is also the only dataset in that table with HDR textures and renderable reflectors. The per-pixel 2D annotation fused onto the mesh and then refined by 3D painting down to individual primitives avoids the boundary errors of Felzenszwalb-based labelling. The qualitative comparison (Fig. 3) shows that clean geometry is what makes clean class and instance renderings possible. There are no ablations or quantitative sim-to-real experiments; realism is argued only through a qualitative 'Replica Turing Test' of raw captures vs renders from the same pose. For navigation, the practical takeaway is that Replica is a small, high-quality Habitat-compatible scene set (it ships a navmesh) suited to evaluation, rendering and perception rather than large-scale agent training.
method: Capture rig + SLAM: custom RGB-D rig with IR structured-light projector records time-aligned IMU, RGB, IR and wide-angle greyscale data. An in-house visual-inertial SLAM system (similar to DSO/ORB-SLAM) provides 6-DoF poses.

Geometry reconstruction: depth is computed from the IR structured-light pattern and fused into a TSDF (KinectFusion-style). Meshes are extracted with Marching Cubes, simplified with Instant Meshes, and textured with a PTex-like per-primitive texture system.

HDR texturing: exposure times of the RGB camera are cycled and per-texel radiance is fused into 16-bit float RGB using the SLAM poses. This gives about 85,000:1 dynamic range (>16 f-stops) versus 8-bit colours in other datasets.

Reflector and hole fixing: mirrors and glass are extracted (Whelan et al. 2018) and manually annotated as planar polygons with a normal and a reflectance value (1 = mirror, otherwise glass). Holes are detected automatically as closed cycles of boundary edges, then filled by an annotator using Liepa's method via CGAL (triangulate, refine, smooth).

Semantic annotation: images are rendered so every primitive is seen at least once, and 2D instance masks are drawn in parallel. Masks are fused onto the mesh by voting and refined with superpixel-like segmentation. A final review uses a 3D mesh-painting tool at primitive-level precision. Privacy regions to be anonymised are also annotated.

Segmentation forest: a hierarchical multi-tree representation with leaves = mesh primitives, middle level = segments and roots = object instances. Class segmentation is obtained by colouring instances by class, and rendering at different levels gives different segmentations. A planar/non-planar pre-segmentation (preseg) is stored in the same format.

Release format and tooling: per scene the release contains mesh.ply, PTex HDR textures, glass.sur, semantic.json/.bin and preseg.json/.bin. A Habitat export provides mesh_semantic.ply, a navmesh and an instance-to-class map. A minimal C++ rendering SDK is included, and Habitat renders RGB, depth and semantics at up to 10k FPS.

numbers_note: Dataset paper with no embodied navigation (or any learning) experiments. The only quantitative content is the dataset statistics in Table 1 (e.g., colour resolution 92k pixels/m², geometry resolution 6k primitives/m², HDR dynamic range ~85,000:1). The scene and class counts are LaTeX macros (\nMesh, \nClass) that are not expanded in the source text; the scene count (18) is inferred from the figure captions.
results: This is a dataset release, not a method, so no benchmark numbers are reported. Table 1 claims higher geometry resolution than Matterport3D (6k vs 0.7k primitives/m² median), comparable colour resolution (92k vs 97k pixels/m²), and HDR textures and reflectors that no other reconstruction dataset has. Qualitative renders (Fig. 3) show cleaner geometry and semantic boundaries than ScanNet and Matterport3D. The raw-vs-render 'Turing test' (Fig. 2) suggests near-photorealism; the renders are given away only by small artifacts and the absence of motion blur.
limitations: Very small scale (18 scenes, mostly single rooms or apartments) compared with Matterport3D (90), Gibson (572) and ScanNet (1,513). This limits its use as a training set for generalisable embodied agents.
No quantitative evidence of the claimed sim-to-real transfer: realism is shown only qualitatively, and no navigation tasks, episodes or baselines are defined.

Scenes are static, non-interactive meshes (no articulated or movable objects, no physics). The 6 FRL-apartment rearrangements are the only temporal variation, and dataset creation relies on heavy manual cleanup, which hinders scaling.
builds_on: Reconstructing mirrors and glass (Whelan et al. 2018)
